title: Thus have I heard
hookLine: "ok so, word for word, here's what she said": the discourses open the same way
tomorrow: why do people say one word three times after a gift?

lines: WORD FOR WORD, HERE'S WHAT SHE SAID.
cards: Ok so. Word for word. Here's exactly what she said.
Somebody in the group retells a conversation like that, and everybody leans in, because the retelling stands or falls on one thing: were you actually there? Now, an older room.

After the Buddha's death, his monks gather at Rajagaha with a big job: say everything he taught, out loud, together, so it won't drift. Maha Kassapa asks the questions. Upali answers on the rules for monks.
Then Kassapa turns to Ananda, the Buddha's attendant, who had heard so many of those talks. Where was this teaching given? To whom?

teach.h: EVAM ME SUTAM: THUS HAVE I HEARD.
teach.b: Tradition says Ananda began each answer with four words of Pali: evam me sutam. Evam, thus. Me, by me.
Sutam, heard. In Rhys Davids' translation: "Thus have I heard."
Then comes the where and the who: at one time the Blessed One was staying near such a town, with such people. Look at what that opening does. It doesn't say: here's what I think.
It doesn't say: here's the truth, trust me.
It says: this is what I heard, and here's where I heard it.

teach.h: A LINE OF PEOPLE WHO HEARD.
teach.b: A source line, before a single teaching is given. The speaker steps aside and points at the moment. So the opening repeats, discourse after discourse, like a librarian's stamp.
It also leaves a little room for honesty. Heard, not invented. Passed on, not owned.
When a monk or a grandmother or a teenager at a temple chants a discourse today, they say it too, evam me sutam, and step into the line of people who heard.

how: When Theravada monks chant a discourse, it opens with evam me sutam, 'thus have I heard', and the place where the Buddha was staying; printed translations of the discourses begin the same way.

games.q: what does “thus have i heard” mean?
o: a closing line monks say when a chant is finished
the vow a monk speaks when he first joins the sangha
the source line that opens the Buddha's discourses

games.q: the council and the opening — tap the pairs.
p: answered on the rules for monks
answered with where, and to whom

s: the 'I' in 'thus have I heard' is the Buddha
the I is the one who heard. tradition says Ananda, the Buddha's attendant.
in the council story, Ananda is asked where each teaching was given, and to whom
Kassapa asks; Ananda answers with the place and the people, before the teaching.
evam me sutam means 'this is what I believe'
evam, thus; me, by me; sutam, heard. a source line, not an opinion.

games.q: at a family dinner you retell a story your grandmother told about her childhood, and you're fuzzy on a few details. what's the evam me sutam way?
o: fill in the gaps so it flows; nobody will check.
tell it as you heard it from her, and say which parts you're unsure of.
don't tell it at all unless you can prove every word.
games.why: thus have I heard: name the source, pass on what you heard, and don't dress up what you didn't.

practice: Write evam me sutam at the top of a page or a note. Under it, write one thing someone told you that you want to keep, and who told you. Say evam me sutam once out loud, read your line back slowly, and sit with it.

wordCard.voice: Thus have I heard: evam me sutam. The opening of the discourses, a source line that says heard, not invented.

orig.note: Pali, in Devanagari letters: evam, thus; me, by me; sutam, heard.

carryVoice: Your line: evam me sutam. Say where it came from, then pass it on. Day 1450, heard and kept.

sources.ref: Vinaya, Cullavagga XI.1 (the council at Rajagaha): Maha Kassapa questions Upali on the Vinaya and Ananda on the Dhamma, asking where each was spoken and about whom
